extracted.intended_audience: employers, workplace safety managers, occupational health & safety compliance officers, and stakeholder commenters on OSHA rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and proposed regulatory requirements for employer controls, break areas, fan use, and acclimatization to prevent heat-related illness under OSHA's proposed heat standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Break area size and availability
rubrics_metrics.description: Break area(s) must be large enough to accommodate the number of employees on rest breaks and be readily available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies to both outdoor and indoor break areas. Employers must ensure spaces can accommodate all employees on break (e.g., sufficient square footage). Break areas should be readily accessible (e.g., unlocked). OSHA requests comment on whether to further specify square footage per employee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Outdoor shade requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers may provide shaded break areas (natural or artificial), but must ensure shade provides effective cooling and is adequate for all employees on break.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shade from buildings, trees, or artificial structures is permitted if reasonably accessible and if employers consider path of shade movement throughout the day to maintain coverage. Employers should not use shaded locations that create safety risks (e.g., tractors/vehicles causing run-over hazards). OSHA asks whether its definition of shade is appropriate and whether situations exist where shade is not protective (e.g., high winds for artificial shade) or when trees/equipment/large vehicles are inappropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Air-conditioned break area criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: A break area can be an air-conditioned enclosed space (e.g., trailer, vehicle, structure) if it is large enough for employees on break and readily available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employers using air-conditioned vehicles must ensure vehicles remain readily available when heat trigger met. For mobile employees, breaks in air-conditioned establishments (convenience store, restaurant) are acceptable if other break-area requirements are met. OSHA requests comments on whether to define levels at which air-conditioning must operate and whether to require pre-cooling of break rooms/vehicles prior to breaks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indoor break area environmental requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Indoor break areas must be air-conditioned or have increased air movement and, if appropriate, de-humidification; must accommodate the number of employees on break and be readily accessible to work area(s).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Break areas can be separate rooms or integrated within the main workspace (demarcated by partitions/screens/signage). Employers should ensure employees can enter break areas for heat-related breaks (e.g., keep unlocked). De-humidification is required when relying on increased air movement in high temperature and high humidity environments. Portable AC units, fans, and portable dehumidifiers may be used; permanent systems are not required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaporative (swamp) cooler allowance
rubrics_metrics.description: In arid environments, employers may use evaporative or 'swamp' coolers as a form of air-conditioning to comply with break area/work area requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaporative coolers are not effective in humid environments. OSHA notes they are acceptable where appropriate (arid climates) and that portable units may be used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indoor work area control options
rubrics_metrics.description: Each indoor work area reasonably expected to meet or exceed the initial heat trigger must be equipped with at least one control option: increased air movement (and de-humidification if appropriate), air-conditioning, or other measures for radiant heat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employers must determine which work areas are expected to meet/exceed the trigger and select controls accordingly. Employers may implement controls for entire spaces or targeted areas where employees are present. Combining controls is allowed. OSHA seeks input on effectiveness specifications and whether to require controls in areas where high ambient temps are necessary for the work process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of fans and increased air movement
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers may use fans (overhead, portable, industrial) or increased ventilation to increase air movement to cool work or break areas, provided natural ventilation produces air movement comparable to fans and does not increase temperature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptable fan options include ceiling fans, portable floor fans, high-velocity fans along aisles, adjustable/oscillating fans, overhead fans, or fans on stands. Employers should consider facility layout, equipment placement, and obstructions when positioning fans. Natural ventilation is acceptable only if it produces equivalent air movement; it is not acceptable if it increases work area temperature.

rubrics_metrics.name: De-humidification when relying on fans
rubrics_metrics.description: When employers rely on increased air movement (fans) in humid environments, they must decrease humidity levels where appropriate (i.e., provide de-humidification).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humidity directly impacts evaporative cooling; modern AC integrates de-humidification, so OSHA requires de-humidification only in high temperature and high humidity environments when employers rely on fans. Employers should consult the fan-use evaluation (paragraph e(6)) to determine when de-humidification is appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fan-use evaluation at high ambient temperatures
rubrics_metrics.description: When ambient temperatures exceed 102 °F (39.0 °C), employers using fans must evaluate humidity levels and discontinue fan use if it is determined that fan use is harmful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA proposes a table (derived from Foster et al., 2022a) mapping ambient temperature rows (e.g., 102.2 °F, 104 °F … >113 °F) to humidity ranges where fan use is allowed vs when fans should be turned off (or discontinued entirely >113 °F). Employers can identify the row matching ambient temperature and check the corresponding allowed humidity range. OSHA acknowledges model limitations (clothing assumptions, sweat rate, fan speed) and is soliciting comments on whether to include such a table or require alternative cooling methods when fans are harmful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition/limits on fan use at extreme temperatures
rubrics_metrics.description: At ambient temperatures above the highest table row (>113.0 °F / >45 °C), OSHA indicates employers should discontinue all fan use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA notes empirical/model limitations and that in some cases (e.g., work clothing) fans may never be beneficial at or above certain temperatures (e.g., 45 °C). Employers should evaluate conditions and use alternative cooling when fans are harmful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Radiant heat-specific controls
rubrics_metrics.description: For indoor work areas with radiant heat sources, employers may use controls (shielding/barriers, isolation, insulation, distance, process modification) that effectively reduce employee exposure to radiant heat instead of fans or air-conditioning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include radiant-reflecting shielding, thermal insulation on hot pipes/surfaces, increasing distance between employees and heat sources, and modifying hot processes. If employers choose these controls in lieu of AC/fans, they must demonstrably reduce exposure to radiant heat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment requirement to identify areas meeting heat trigger
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers are expected to determine which indoor work areas are reasonably expected to meet or exceed the initial heat trigger and apply controls to those areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment considerations include proximity to heat-generating machinery, nature of heat source, and workspace configuration. For areas at or above trigger (e.g., near ovens, kilns), employers must implement one or more of the prescribed control options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptable indoor break area location and demarcation
rubrics_metrics.description: Indoor break areas need not be separate rooms; they can be integrated into the main workspace provided they are demarcated and allow effective cooling and hydration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demarcation can be via partitions, screens, or signage. If sensitive/hazardous work prevents establishing a break area in main room, employers may provide a separate readily accessible area. Control booths/rooms (if accessible and meeting size/location requirements) may qualify as break areas; locked/restricted booths do not qualify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acclimatization for new employees — Option A (high-heat measures)
rubrics_metrics.description: For new employees during first week, Option A requires implementing the measures required at the high heat trigger (paragraph f) whenever the initial heat trigger is met or exceeded during that week.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measures (per paragraph f) include a minimum 15-minute paid rest break at least every two hours in a compliant break area, observation for signs/symptoms of heat-related illness, and providing hazard alerts with specified information about prevention and seeking help. Option A is intended as an alternative when gradual acclimatization may be impractical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acclimatization for new employees — Option B (gradual exposure)
rubrics_metrics.description: For new employees during first week, Option B requires gradual heat exposure: restrict exposure to no more than 20% of a normal work shift on day 1 and increase exposure by no more than 20% of the work shift on each subsequent day (days 2–4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employers may meet this by assigning non-heat-exposed tasks (training, paperwork, office work) or task replacement. If the initial heat trigger is exceeded only for portion(s) of a shift, exposure coordination should match those periods. Employers must implement acclimatization protocols at no cost to employees (cannot remove pay or use paid leave to cover unexposed hours).

rubrics_metrics.name: Acclimatization for returning employees (>14 days) — Option A and B
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers must implement either Option A (measures at high heat trigger during first week back) or Option B (gradual exposure: 50% of normal shift on day 1, 60% on day 2, 80% on day 3) for employees returning after more than 14 days away.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employers may satisfy gradual exposure by reassigning work to non-heat tasks. Shift schedules with <14 days off (e.g., two weeks on/two weeks off) are not covered by this requirement if the off period does not exceed 14 days. OSHA requests comment on whether to require acclimatization during heat waves or annual acclimatization at season start.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exception to acclimatization requirement for 'same or similar conditions'
rubrics_metrics.description: Exception applies if employee consistently worked under the same or similar tasks and heat conditions within the prior 14 days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Same or similar conditions' means tasks similar or higher in exertion and similar or hotter heat conditions (e.g., heat index at or above current job). 'Consistently' is intended as at least two hours per day on a majority of the preceding 14 days. Employers should not assume similar climates by country; they may check weather records. Examples distinguish similar vs dissimilar tasks (e.g., picking tomatoes vs watermelons; manual trench digging vs machine trenching). OSHA requests comments on clarity of this term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification standard for acclimatization exception
rubrics_metrics.description: To rely on the 14-day 'same or similar conditions' exception, employers must obtain supporting details from the employee (timing, location, duration, type of work); a single yes/no without supporting details is insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employers may ask verbally or in writing but must document sufficient information to demonstrate the employee engaged in similar tasks in similar heat for the required duration and frequency.

rubrics_metrics.name: No-cost requirement for acclimatization protocols
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers must implement acclimatization protocols at no cost to employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employers may not relieve employees from duty during acclimatization and not pay them, nor may employers require employees to use paid leave to cover hours not worked for acclimatization purposes. Benefits are considered compensation and cannot be used to cover unworked hours during acclimatization.
